CFTC's First Innovation Panel Zeroes In on Prediction Market Manipulation

Published August 22, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission held the first meeting of its new Innovation Advisory Committee on Thursday, August 21, drawing roughly 30 executives from exchanges, prediction market platforms, crypto firms, and sports betting operators — and manipulation risk in event contracts, the regulated instruments underlying platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket, dominated the discussion.

What was said

CME Group CEO Terry Duffy pushed the group to take manipulation vulnerabilities seriously, arguing the industry needs stronger safeguards around event contracts. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig pushed back on some of the specific concerns raised, noting that certain cited incidents involved offshore platforms outside the CFTC's direct jurisdiction. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong proposed a three-step framework for evaluating whether a novel contract should be allowed to list in the first place.

Committee members pointed to several already-public incidents as evidence of the risk: a White House aide who profited more than $100,000 trading Kalshi contracts on which specific words President Trump would say in speeches; a U.S. Army master sergeant who made over $400,000 trading a contract tied to Nicolás Maduro's capture using what was described as insider knowledge; and former congressman George Santos, who was fined $35,000 over a contract tied to his own attendance at a State of the Union address.

Why it matters for bettors

Prediction markets have expanded rapidly since self-certification became the norm for listing new contracts — roughly 2,500 contracts have been self-certified since January 2025 with zero CFTC objections, according to figures discussed at the meeting. Duffy argued some of those contracts likely run afoul of the CFTC's Core Principle 3, which requires safeguards against manipulation. The committee's scrutiny lands as prediction market platforms increasingly overlap with traditional sports betting, competing for the same customers and, in some states, drawing the same kind of regulatory pushback that has already led to platform restrictions elsewhere this year.

The CFTC itself is currently operating with only one sitting commissioner, Selig, well below its full five-member structure, which could shape how quickly any new manipulation safeguards actually get formalized.
